clinical_knowledge.topic: Infective Endocarditis of the Aortic Valve (IV drug use) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Infective Endocarditis of the Aortic Valve (IV drug use) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes targeted high-dose IV anti-staphylococcal therapy for MSSA, with regimen selection guided by microbiology, renal function, allergy history, and surgical planning, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: chills, night sweats, weight loss, and new regurgitant heart murmur with mobile vegetation on echocardiogram

Key HPI features: 53M with history of intravenous drug use presents with 3-week history of high fevers, drenching night sweats, 15-lb weight loss, generalized weakness, and painful reddish spots on the pads of his fingers. Over the past 3 days, developed worsening shortness of breath and ankle swelling.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 110, BP 105/50 (wide pulse pressure), Temp 39.1C. Splinter hemorrhages under nail beds, tender Osler nodes on finger pads, painless Janeway lesions on palms. Auscultation reveals a loud Grade 3/6 blowing diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation at left sternal border. Three sets of blood cultures positive for Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-sensitive MSSA). Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) reveals a 1.6 cm highly mobile, destructive vegetation attached to the aortic valve leaflets with perforation of the right coronary cusp causing severe acute aortic regurgitation and a 1.2 cm perivalvular aortic root abscess.
Relevant background/PMH: Hepatitis C, active IV heroin/fentanyl injection drug use
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Infective Endocarditis of the Aortic Valve (IV drug use).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: New heart failure symptoms (breathlessness, ankle swelling) with fever — suggests severe valve destruction needing urgent surgery.
management_principles: Treat MSSA with targeted high-dose IV anti-staphylococcal therapy (e.g., nafcillin/oxacillin or cefazolin as appropriate); routine synergistic gentamicin is not recommended because nephrotoxicity outweighs unproven benefit

STAT emergency cardiothoracic surgery consultation for urgent operative intervention: aortic root reconstruction and aortic valve replacement with cryopreserved homograft or mechanical/bioprosthetic valve
Surgical indications present: severe acute AR with heart failure, perivalvular root abscess, and large mobile vegetation > 10 mm with embolization risk
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

Auscultation reveals a loud Grade 3/6 blowing diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation at left sternal border. reference_soap.assessment: Severe Infective Endocarditis of the Aortic Valve due to MSSA complicated by leaflet destruction, acute severe aortic regurgitation, and aortic root abscess.
reference_soap.plan: Treat MSSA with targeted high-dose IV anti-staphylococcal therapy (e.g., nafcillin/oxacillin or cefazolin as appropriate); routine synergistic gentamicin is not recommended because nephrotoxicity outweighs unproven benefit. STAT emergency cardiothoracic surgery consultation for urgent operative intervention: aortic root reconstruction and aortic valve replacement with cryopreserved homograft or mechanical/bioprosthetic valve. Surgical indications present: severe acute AR with heart failure, perivalvular root abscess, and large mobile vegetation > 10 mm with embolization risk.

learning_objectives: Identify clinical criteria and peripheral immunological/embolic stigmata of Infective Endocarditis (Modified Duke criteria, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots)

Recognize critical indications for emergent/urgent cardiothoracic surgical valve replacement in endocarditis (refractory heart failure, perivalvular abscess/fistula, persistent bacteremia, large mobile vegetations >10-15 mm)
Compare prosthetic valve selection options (mechanical vs bioprosthetic vs homograft) in active endocarditis and IV drug use
Outline multidisciplinary management combining prolonged targeted IV antimicrobial therapy with complex root debridement/reconstruction

teaching.diagnosis: Infective Endocarditis of the Aortic Valve (IV drug use)
teaching.one_liner: Bacteria introduced through injection drug use seed the aortic valve, destroying the leaflets and causing severe regurgitation, heart failure symptoms, and peripheral immune stigmata like Osler's nodes.
differentials: Sepsis from a skin/soft tissue source
red_flags: New heart failure symptoms (breathlessness, ankle swelling) with fever — suggests severe valve destruction needing urgent surgery

must_ask.say: Can you tell me about your drug use — what you use and how often you inject?
How long have you had fevers and night sweats?
Have you noticed any tender spots on your fingertips?
Have you had trouble breathing or swelling in your ankles?
How much weight have you lost?

history.answer: I've been having high fevers and waking up drenched in cold sweat for the past three weeks, and now I feel completely wiped out and short of breath.
The fever started about three weeks ago and has been coming back almost every day since.
My temperature went over 102 degrees at home, and I get intense shaking chills whenever it spikes.
I took some over-the-counter acetaminophen, but it only lowered the fever for a couple of hours before it shot right back up.
I don't have a cough or sore throat, but over the last three days I have gotten noticeably short of breath just walking across the room.
No, I haven't had any burning when I pee, no need to go frequently, and no flank pain.
No, I haven't had any belly pain, nausea, vomiting, or loose stools.
No severe headaches, my neck feels normal and not stiff, and I haven't felt confused.
I noticed these painful red bumps on my fingertips and red spots on my palms, but no tick bites, black scabs, or joint pains.
Yes, I wake up soaked in sweat having to change my clothes, and my clothes are loose because I've lost about fifteen pounds.
No, I haven't felt any swollen lumps in my neck, armpits, or groin.
No, I haven't traveled anywhere, haven't been hiking or working outdoors, and haven't been around animals.
No, none of my friends or acquaintances have been running fevers or sick like this.
No, I have never had chemotherapy and I don't take steroids or medications that suppress my immune system.
I've never been told I have heart problems or an artificial valve, and I haven't had any dental work or surgical procedures lately.
history.topic: Prior heart disease and dental procedures

history.answer: No, I haven't started taking any new prescription pills.
I regularly inject heroin and fentanyl into my veins, and sometimes I've had to reuse or share needles.
I haven't had any new sexual partners recently, and I have no history of sexually transmitted infections.
Besides those tender spots on my fingertips, I noticed some thin dark lines under my fingernails that look like splinters.
Over the last three days both of my ankles have swollen up, and I have to prop myself up on extra pillows at night to breathe.
I honestly thought I had caught a horrible case of the flu or picked up a bad infection in my bloodstream.
I'm really worried about these tender bumps on my fingers and why I'm struggling so much to catch my breath.
I want to be admitted to the hospital and given strong IV antibiotics to knock this infection out.
I have chronic Hepatitis C from injecting drugs, but no history of diabetes, high blood pressure, or asthma.
I've never had any operations, and I haven't been admitted to a hospital before.
I don't take any regular prescribed medicines, herbal supplements, or vitamins.
I don't have any known allergies to antibiotics or other medications.
I smoke about half a pack of cigarettes a day and have smoked for over twenty years.
I drink a couple of beers on the weekend, but I don't drink hard liquor or binge drink.
I'm currently unemployed and staying with a friend in an apartment.
My father had high blood pressure, but there is no family history of early heart valve conditions or sudden cardiac death.

exam.finding: Ill-appearing, diaphoretic, flushed man resting in bed in mild respiratory distress.
Blood pressure 105/50 mmHg, pulse 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 96% on ambient air.
Oropharynx is clear without mucosal erythema, petechiae, or tonsillar exudates.
No cervical, supraclavicular, or submandibular lymphadenopathy palpable.
Bilateral fine end-inspiratory crackles heard at the lung bases without wheezes.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with a loud Grade 3/6 blowing early diastolic murmur heard best at the left sternal border.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender throughout with no guarding or rebound.
Tender erythematous nodules on the finger pads, painless erythematous macules on the palms, splinter hemorrhages under nail beds, and venipuncture track marks in the antecubital fossae.
Bilateral 1+ pitting pretibial and ankle edema.
Neck is supple with negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
